facts: The first machine age (Industrial Revolution): machines automate or augment physical tasks; the second: cognitive tasks.
The authors advise people to race with the machine, not against it, aiming for machines that complement humans rather than substitute for them.
Software grades essays more objectively, consistently and quickly than humans.
Kasparov (NYRB 2010) on a 2005 Playchess.com freestyle tournament: winners were two amateur Americans using three computers at once.
Kasparov's formula: weak human plus machine plus better process beat a strong computer alone and a strong human plus machine plus inferior process.
One report names the winning team ZackS, two amateurs from New Hampshire, who beat a 14-year-old Russian grandmaster 2.5-1.5 in the final; their edge was directing the search effectively.
A commentator notes that computers may become strong enough that a human adds nothing (as in checkers); humans add value by pruning variations, spotting where programs disagree, managing time.
Kenneth Regan's data (via a blog post): a striking share of the most accurate games ever played came from human-computer teams; Forbes.com earnings previews are generated by algorithms.
tension: Amateurs with a better process beat stronger players and stronger computers.
opening_idea: Open on the two amateurs using three computers at once.
